synopsis: The strategy requires testing the new collision-mitigation system in the same virtual environments as the baseline, but fair comparison rests on common system outputs in world or risk coordinates—not raw sensor statistics when sensors, mounting or processing differ [f26, f105, f107, f5211]. The strongest experiment records both sensor suites simultaneously on one machine against an independent reference trajectory; separate deployments confound site, operator and weather, and mounting interference must itself be tested [f5509, f5482, f5511, f14364]. Common measures include warnings and interventions per hazard, missed hazards, false and nuisance alarms per hour under equal exposure, and warning timing against common ground truth and a shared hazard zone; calibrated ground truth is essential because verdict errors can dominate system differences [f106, f5478, f7474]. The old fleet supplies the warning-performance baseline, including false and nuisance alarm rates to beat, but this is not the assurance target for automatic braking: only common warning stages are directly comparable, while braking must meet new hazard-derived requirements and be assessed in closed loop [f11783, f11906, f10529, f14363]. Replay supports comparison only with genuinely equivalent inputs, and the corpus reports unresolved evidence gaps, including missing exposure denominators for accident comparisons and no apples-to-apples stopping-distance accuracy benchmark across tools on the same production machines [f5238, f5512, f3658, f6397].
